title: A temple (1 Corinthians 6:19–20)
hook: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost

segments.voice: Yesterday, coadjutors: Paul planting and Apollos watering. Your line was god gives the increase. Did you do your small part, and let go? Day five hundred seventy-one.

A body can be treated like a machine, pushed past every warning light: no sleep, no lunch, one more coffee. Or like a project, to fix, judge, compare and criticize in the mirror. Or, on a good week, like a sturdy thing that simply carries a person through the day. None of these treats it as holy. Corinth had its own version of this argument about the body. And Paul answers it with a startling sentence.
screen: `A MACHINE TO PUSH.` → `A PROJECT TO CRITICIZE.` → `OR: SOMETHING HOLY?`

segments.voice: Some Corinthians, it seems, had a slogan: everything is permitted to me. The body doesn't really matter; it's the spirit that counts. So what you do with your body, in eating, in sex, is spiritually neutral. Paul disagrees, strongly. In the Douay-Rheims: "Or know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own?" To Paul's first readers, a temple was a sacred place. In Jerusalem, the Temple's innermost room was, in Israel's faith, where God's presence dwelt. The Greek word Paul uses here, naos, usually points to the sanctuary itself rather than the whole complex with its courtyards. Paul is saying: the holiest room is you. Your body. Not just your soul. Then: "For you are bought with a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body." Bought with a price: the language of the marketplace, which some readers hear as a slave set free by someone paying. On that reading, not being your own isn't a burden: someone paid a great price. The setting is honest: Paul is warning here about sexual immorality, and he means it seriously. But the reason he gives reaches every part of bodily life. Catholics take this into how they think about the body: it will rise again at the resurrection, the Eucharist is received into it, and it is to be neither worshiped nor despised. Saint John Paul the Second built a whole series of teachings, the theology of the body, on this conviction. A temple isn't a machine or a project. You take care of it, because someone lives there.
screen: `EVERYTHING IS PERMITTED?` · `NAOS: THE INNER SANCTUARY.` · `BOUGHT WITH A PRICE.` · `NOT WORSHIPED, NOT DESPISED.` · then, large: `YOUR BODY IS THE TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rest your body today. Settle, and breathe. Start at your feet and move slowly upward. Notice where you're holding tension: jaw, shoulders, the back of the neck. Breathe into each place and let it soften a little. Don't judge anything you find. Just notice, the way you'd walk quietly through a church. Then pick one way to care for your body today: a real meal, a walk, water, going to bed on time. If you pray, you can thank God for the body you have, exactly as it is. The bell holds the time.
A temple. Paul's word for the body: the inner sanctuary where the Holy Spirit lives, bought with a price, and worth caring for. Today's word.
Your line: bought with a price. Today, give your body one real act of rest or care, as if someone lives there. Day five hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Catholics believe the Holy Spirit dwells in the baptized, profess the resurrection of the body in the Creed, and care for the body through rest on Sunday, moderation, and reverence for the bodies of the dead.

fork.setup: you're Paul. some in Corinth say the body is spiritually irrelevant, so anything goes. what do you say?
options: agree; the spirit is what counts.
say the body is the Spirit's temple, bought with a price.
tell them to punish the body instead.
fork.reveal: neither indulgence nor contempt: your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, you are not your own, so glorify God in your body.

original.note: Greek: temple, specifically the inner sanctuary where the god was thought to dwell.

trapdoor: what you thought: take care of your health, it's a gift.
what it means: the body is the holiest room, where the Holy Spirit lives, and it was bought at a price.
what a scholar hears: Paul chose naos, the inner shrine, not hieron, the temple complex. earlier in this letter he calls the whole church God's temple; here he says it of each body.

sources.quoted: Or know you not, that your members are the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is in you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own?
For you are bought with a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of 1 Corinthians 6:19–20. 'And in your spirit, which are God's' (6:20) is in the KJV's Greek base but absent from the oldest manuscripts and from the Vulgate/Douay; a Keeper may prefer quoting only the first half of 6:20.
'Everything is permitted to me' (6:12) is widely read as a Corinthian slogan Paul quotes; confirm.
Naos vs hieron distinction: standard; confirm.
John Paul II's Theology of the Body (Wednesday audiences 1979–1984): confirm phrasing.
CCC 364 (body as temple of the Spirit) and 1004: confirm.

Reviewer softened three claims in the teach: the 'everything is permitted' slogan ('it seems'), naos 'usually points to' the sanctuary (naos can also mean the temple building generally), and 'bought with a price' as slave-market imagery ('many readers hear'): whether Paul means purchase by a new owner or ransom into freedom is debated.

Editor review (2026-10-01): 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 now quoted from the Douay-Rheims ('your members are the temple'; 'bought with a great price. Glorify and bear God in your body'), not the KJV, which also settles the earlier note on 'and in your spirit'. Hook no longer says 'most of us' or 'one of the most surprising sentences'; 'the most sacred place there was' softened; God's presence in the Temple framed as Israel's faith. Douay wording checked against drbo.org.
